Below is a focused 3-week powerlifting peaking block designed to taper volume, maintain intensity, and have the client fresh and ready for a meet in 21 days. It assumes the client is intermediate, has completed 12 weeks of accumulation, and will compete in classic powerlifting (squat, bench, deadlift). Program goals: reduce total training volume, keep top-end intensities (heavy singles/doubles) to maintain neural readiness, practice openers and planned attempts, manage recovery and nutrition, and reduce fatigue so the athlete is fresh on meet day.

General guidelines before the plan
- Maxes / percentages: Use the athlete’s current training maxes (TM) or recent single maxes from the 12-week block. If you prefer percentages of an 1RM, use those; otherwise use the heaviest singles done in the last 2–3 weeks as references.
- Intensity: Maintain high intensity (85–98% of 1RM) for main lifts in weeks 1–2 but reduce total volume (sets × reps). Week 3 is the competition week: very low volume, some very light/intensity rehearsal for openers and planned attempts.
- RPE: Keep main heavy singles around RPE 8–9 in week 1–2 and RPE 7–8 in week 3 for rehearsals—avoid crushing grinders the week of the meet.
- Frequency: Keep usual training frequency (3–4 sessions/week) depending on the client; the plan below assumes 3 main lifting days per week (Squat day, Bench day, Deadlift day) with accessory work limited and recovery-focused.
- Warm-ups: Thorough movement-specific warm-up + ramp sets before heavy work. Keep ramping systematic: long enough to be ready but not to induce fatigue.
- Rest and recovery: 3–6 minutes between heavy sets/singles, 2–3 minutes for heavy doubles/triples. Sleep 8+ hours when possible, cold shower/contrast baths only if client uses them, mobility and breathing work daily.
- Nutrition: Maintain calories at or slightly above maintenance during peaking to support strength and recovery (avoid large deficits). Carb-timing: emphasize carbs before heavy sessions and the day before the meet. Hydration and sodium management per client’s usual strategy for bodyweight. Protein ~1.6–2.0 g/kg/day. During last 48 hours before weigh-ins, follow the client’s established weight-making strategy if any—do not experiment.
- Mental prep: Practice meet commands (pause on bench, depth on squat if needed), visualization, and cue phrases. Record attempts in week 2 heavy sessions to evaluate opener selection.
- Meet week travel: If traveling, do light movements, maintain sleep, and get in early arrival when possible.

Three-week plan overview
- Week 1 (Day 1–7): Peaking start — intensity high (85–95% singles/doubles), volume reduced ~50% from accumulation. Heavy day per lift with one top single or double; accessory reduced to maintain technique and confidence.
- Week 2 (Day 8–14): Near-peak — intensity held (90–98% for planned heavy singles), even lower volume. Work up to heavy singles that mimic planned openers and second attempts. Record or evaluate to set meet attempts. Reduce accessory further.
- Week 3 (Day 15–21): Competition week — very low volume, minimal intensity re-tests, walk-throughs and sharpness. Two light sessions early in the week with openers rehearsed. Final 48–72 hours taper to passive recovery, mobility, and mental focus. Meet day: follow warm-up protocol and attempt plan.

Detailed week-by-week plan
Notes: “Main sets” list percentages based on 1RM. Replace with the client’s numbers. Accessory sets are kept short and light (about 40–60% 1RM or RPE 5–6), focused on competition-specific weaknesses and movement quality.

Week 1 (Day 1–7) — Start taper, maintain heavy intensity
Session A — Squat focus (Day 1)
- Warm-up: 10–15 min general + specific mobility, bodyweight squats, banded activation.
- Ramp: 5–6 ramp sets to working weight.
- Main: Work up to 1 heavy single at 90–95% 1RM (or an RPE 8–9 single). No AMRAP. If feeling very sharp, you may do a double at 85–90% instead.
  - Example: 3–4 ramp sets, then 1 × 1 @ 92–95%.
- Back-off: 2 × 3 @ 80% (easy, pause for depth check if needed).
- Accessory (short): 2 × 8 Romanian deadlift light (50–60% effort) for posterior chain, 2 × 12 single-leg RDL or glute bridge to keep hamstrings/glutes primed.
- Core: 2 × 30–45s plank.
- Duration: ~50–60 min.

Session B — Bench focus (Day 3)
- Warm-up: thoracic mobility, band shoulder prep, scapular work.
- Ramp: 4–6 ramp sets.
- Main: Heavy double or single at 88–95% 1RM (choose double if confidence is high and technique remains good). Eg. 1 × 2 @ 88–90% or 1 × 1 @ 92–95%.
- Back-off: 2 × 3–5 @ 75–80% (touch-and-go optional depending on meet rules; practice paused bench if meet requires).
- Accessory (short): 2 × 8–10 incline DB press (moderate), 2 × 8–12 face pulls for shoulder health.
- Triceps: 2 × 10 pushdowns light.
- Duration: ~50 min.

Session C — Deadlift focus (Day 5)
- Warm-up: hip mobility, hamstring activation, light sled pulls if available.
- Ramp: 5 ramp sets.
- Main: Work up to 1 heavy single at 90–95% 1RM. Alternatively, heavy double at 85–90% if technique allows.
  - Example: 1 × 1 @ 92–95%.
- Back-off: 2 × 3 @ 80% conventional/Sumo depending on competition style.
- Accessory: 2 × 6–8 weighted back extensions or 2 × 6–8 deficit pulls at moderate load (not to failure). Keep volume low.
- Core: 2 × 20–30s heavy-loaded carry (farmer carry) or anti-rotation hold.
- Duration: ~50–60 min.

Recovery work between sessions (days off)
- Active recovery: 20–30 min light cardio, mobility work, foam rolling.
- Sleep priority and nutrition focus described above.

Week 2 (Day 8–14) — Near-peak; test heavy singles for attempt selection
Session A — Squat (Day 8)
- Warm-up: mobility and ramp sets.
- Main: Work up to 1–2 singles: planned opener (usually ~90% of planned 1RM?) and a planned second attempt (95–98% if confident). The goal is to practice opener and second attempt ranges — but do NOT grind a near-max unless confident in technique and recovery. Practical example: 1 × 1 @ 90%, then 1 × 1 @ 95% (stop if very close to true 1RM or if it feels heavy).
- Back-off: 2 × 2 @ 80% (light and technical).
- Accessory: 2 × 8 paused goblet squats or box squats light for depth; leg curls 2 × 10 if needed.
- Keep session ~45–60 min.

Session B — Bench (Day 10)
- Warm-up: bands, scapular work, 5–6 ramp sets.
- Main: Practice opener as single and second attempt single if confident. Example: 1 × 1 @ 90% (opener), then 1 × 1 @ 95% (second) if technique is perfect; otherwise stop after opener. Avoid max-out that leaves soreness.
- Back-off: 2 × 3 @ 75% paused.
- Accessory: 2 × 10-12 light DB row, 2 × 12 face pulls for balance.
- Keep volume and fatigue low.

Session C — Deadlift (Day 12)
- Warm-up: hip/hamstring prep, ramp sets.
- Main: Work up to planned opener single (e.g., 1 × 1 @ 88–92%), and optionally a heavier single replicating second attempt (95–98%) if technique and recovery are excellent. If client is peaked and confident, record the heavier single to set attempt. If it’s a grind, stop at opener.
- Back-off: 2 × 2 @ 75–80% conventional/Sumo light.
- Accessory: 2 × 8 RDLs light; 2 × 30s core anti-flexion holds.
- Duration: ~45–60 min.

Notes for Week 2: This is the last week to experiment with attempts. Use these heavy singles to set opener, second, and projected third attempts. If any heavy single left the athlete unusually beat up, adjust week 3 accordingly (more rest/light work).

Week 3 (Meet Week, Day 15–21) — Taper to meet day
Goals: Keep sessions very short, sharpen the feel of the lifts, practice openers, stay fresh. Avoid heavy grinding singles. If meet is late in the week, adjust timing so the last heavy-ish work is 3–5 days prior.

Session A — Light Squat/Technique (Day 15 or 16; 5–6 days before meet)
- Warm-up: mobility + nerve/flossing if used.
- Worksets: 3–4 sets of 2–3 reps at 50–60% focusing on speed, technique, and depth (not fatigue). Include 1–2 reps at opener weight once to feel it (single or double, easy).
- Accessory: 2 × 6–8 light glute work or banded lateral work.
- Duration: 30–40 min.

Session B — Light Bench (Day 17 or 18; 3–4 days before meet)
- Warm-up: band and shoulder prep.
- Worksets: 3 × 3 @ 50–60% focusing on touch-and-go/paused depending on meet requirement. Perform 1 rep at opener weight lightly to rehearse commands.
- Accessory: minimal—2 × 12 face pulls, 1 × 10 triceps band work.
- Duration: 25–35 min.

Session C — Light Deadlift (Day 18 or 19; 3–4 days before meet)
- Warm-up: dynamic mobility.
- Worksets: 2–3 × 2 reps at ~50–60%; 1 rep at opener weight if desired (easy, not to failure).
- Accessory: minimal hamstring activation, 2 × 30s core carry.
- Duration: 25–35 min.

Last 48–72 hours before meet
- No heavy lifting. Short mobility, light walks, foam rolling, and visualization. Practice mental routines and breathing. Hydrate well and prioritize carbs the day before competition. If weigh-in is earlier, time carb intake to hit weight and refill glycogen after weigh-in if allowed.
- Sleep: aim for best sleep nights (avoid late-night travel if possible).

Meet day morning
- Follow a tested warm-up routine. Use planned opener, second, and third attempts rehearsed in week 2.
- Keep caffeine and stimulants to usual tolerated levels. Have familiar pre-meet meals (carb-focused breakfast ~3–4 hours before meet or smaller meal 1–2 hours prior depending on stomach tolerance).
- Warm-up sets should be brief and efficient on platform. Arrive early to the venue and manage arousal.

Example attempt selection strategy (use actual recent performance to set numbers)
- Opener: conservative — a weight the athlete can hit for a comfortable triple in training about 90–93% of current 1RM (or 92–95% of current best training single). The idea: secure a good first successful lift.
- Second: 95–97% of 1RM or a weight that is challenging but within the athlete’s near-max single practiced in Week 2.
- Third: an all-out attempt — either a PR if they have the energy or a weight that is realistic given meet-day feeling. Avoid adding large jumps that risk missing badly; incremental increases between attempts are preferred (2.5–5kg depending on the athlete).

Nutrition specifics for the 3-week block (concise)
- Calories: maintain near maintenance or slight surplus (+100–200 kcal) to support recovery. Do not start a diet; avoid big deficits.
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg bodyweight daily.
- Carbohydrates: higher on heavy training days (pre and post workout). During meet week, increase carbs the day before the meet for glycogen topping (~6–8 g/kg if weight allows and heavy long meet energy required).
- Hydration: normal hydration throughout. If competing in a weight class and using dehydration methods, follow their tested plan; do not experiment in final week.
- Supplements: creatine maintained (do not stop), caffeine pre-lift if used regularly, electrolytes for longer meets. Avoid new supplements.

Recovery and readiness checklist
- Sleep 7–9 hours nightly. Nap if needed.
- Light mobility and short walks on rest days.
- Contrast baths/cold tubs only if athlete normally uses them; otherwise focus on passive rest.
- Pain management: address any nagging aches with physio, massage, or targeted mobility early in week 1–2.
- Mental: visualize the meet, rehearse commands, and maintain positive, confidence-based self-talk.

Contingency notes
- If a heavy single in Week 2 causes sustained soreness, drop the remaining Heavy Day intensity and move to lighter, technique-focused sets for the rest of the week.
- If the athlete feels extremely sharp and recovered, keep the heavy singles controlled (no brutal grinders) — they can be slightly heavier, but avoid risking meet readiness.
- If the athlete misses a heavy rep in Week 2, reassess attempt choices and lean slightly more conservative for opener selection.

Summary plan at a glance
- Week 1: Heavy singles at 90–95% on main lifts + minimal back-off work; accessories short.
- Week 2: Test opener and (optionally) second attempts with controlled singles (90–98%) — record to finalize attempt plan; minimal accessories.
- Week 3 (meet week): Very light work, practice openers, rest and recover, carb-load the day before, and be ready for meet day.

Short answer: leave major technical changes alone in the peaking block. Use only minor, well-ingrained cues that the lifter already uses reliably — not new large adjustments.

Why:
- Goal of a peaking block is to reduce fatigue and preserve neuromuscular readiness for the meet. Learning or aggressively changing a movement pattern (like a substantial scapular/shoulder retraction change) increases cognitive and motor demand and can temporarily reduce force output, timing, and confidence.
- Big technical alterations close to a meet raise the risk of missed lifts or awkward attempts under load/pressure.

When to keep the cue:
- If “pull shoulders together more” is already a practiced, comfortable cue the athlete has been using reliably throughout the 12-week accumulation and it doesn’t produce a noticeable weakness or tightness, continue reinforcing it lightly. Small, familiar reminders can help consistency without creating disruption.
- If the cue simply reminds her to keep her usual setup (scapular retraction, chest up) and she’s been performing well with it, maintain it in warm-ups and light rehearsals.

When to back off or delay drilling:
- If the cue is new, poorly executed, or has required concentrated technical drilling during accumulation (i.e., it changed her bar path, timing, or required different motor patterns), avoid intensive drilling in the 3-week peak. Don’t try to relearn scapular mechanics or change grip width/pressing groove now.
- If emphasizing the cue has produced tightness in the upper back or shoulders that compromises arch, punch, or breathing, reduce its use to avoid limiting performance.

How to handle it in this peaking block:
- Practice the cue only in very low-volume, low-intensity settings: warm-ups, specific technical warm-up sets at 50–60% (a few reps), and a single light rehearsal of the opener on bench days in Week 3. Use it as a reminder rather than a technique overhaul.
- Use short, low-effort accessory or activation work to reinforce the position without fatigue: 2 sets of 8–10 band pull-aparts, 2 sets of 6–8 scapular squeezes, or 1–2 sets of 8–10 light paused bench reps at 40–50% focusing on position only. Keep these short and non-fatiguing and perform them early in the session as part of warm-up.
- Use video-only feedback sparingly: a quick phone video of setup once per week can help confirm the cue is producing the desired scapular position; avoid long technical coaching sessions.

Coaching cues to keep it low-risk:
- Frame it as a setup cue: “set the shoulders together and down, breathe and brace, then keep chest up” — short and consistent.
- Use tactile or brief external cues only if she’s comfortable with them and they don’t add stress.
- Remind to prioritize comfort, breathing, and timing over an exaggerated squeeze.

If you want a specific micro-plan for using the cue during the remaining 3 weeks
- Week 1: Continue current cueing during warm-ups and main work; add 1 short activation mini-set per bench day: 1 × 8 band pull-aparts + 1 × 6 light paused reps at 40–50% focusing on shoulder set.
- Week 2: Limit to warm-up and opener rehearsal only. 1 × 5 band pull-aparts early in session; 1 × 1 opener single at planned weight (light) with the cue.
- Week 3 (meet week): Use the cue in walk-throughs only — 2–3 reps at 50–60% during the early-week short session and 1 easy opener rehearsal. No drilling or fatigue-inducing accessory work.

Bottom line: don’t introduce big new technique work now. If the cue is already part of her stable setup and performance, continue it gently. If it’s new or causing issues, delay intensive drilling until after the meet. Below is a clear, practical meet-morning plan you can give your athlete. It assumes a standard powerlifting meet with a morning weigh-in already completed (if not, tell me timing and I’ll adapt). Timing should be adjusted to the meet’s schedule and the athlete’s individual warm-up preferences; use the meet’s reporting time and flight times to set exact minutes. The focus: efficient warm-up, low fatigue, confidence-building, and arriving at the platform ready for the opener.

General principles
- Keep it simple, rehearsed, and time-efficient. Don’t try anything new.
- Warm-up should be progressive but brief — long enough to raise core temp, rehearse motor patterns, and prime nervous system without inducing fatigue.
- Use exact ramp sets in the gym warm-up and only brief platform warm-up before the attempt.
- Stick to the planned attempt selection and small mental rituals (breathing, cues).
- Nutrition/hydration: small, familiar, carb-forward meals. Avoid heavy, fatty, or very high-fiber foods the morning of the meet.

Example timeline (assumes flight/attempt for first lift is ~11:00 and athlete is in the 2nd flight — adapt as needed)
- 06:30–07:00 — Wake, light movement
  - Wake at a consistent time (earlier if travel/venue requires). Start with 2–5 minutes of light movement (walking around hotel room, ankle pumps) to get circulation going.
  - Bathroom, check weigh-in status if relevant, short breathing/visualization (2–3 minutes).

- 07:00–07:30 — Breakfast
  - Small, familiar meal: carbs + moderate protein + small fat. Examples: oatmeal with banana and a scoop of protein or Greek yogurt with honey and toast; or bagel with a little peanut butter and egg whites. Keep it small enough to digest comfortably.
  - Hydrate: 300–500 ml water with electrolytes. Continue sipping water thereafter.
  - If athlete uses caffeine, have typical dose 60–90 minutes before planned warm-up time (not too late if they’re sensitive).

- 07:30–08:30 — Light mobility, mental prep, and rest
  - 10–20 minute easy walk or light cardio (optional — should be very low intensity) to further raise body temp and loosen joints.
  - 5–10 minutes of mobility focusing on hips/shoulders and thoracic extension.
  - 5–10 minutes visualization: run through the meet run-order, opener successful lifts, cues (shoulder set, tight arch, leg drive, breathing).
  - Put gear (singlet, socks) in the bag and confirm warm-up order/time with coach/athlete.

- 09:00–10:00 — Travel to venue / check-in arrival buffer
  - Arrive early. Check athlete list, look at platform and warm-up area, identify nearest bathroom and food area.
  - Start sipping a carb drink or small snack (e.g., half a banana, small energy bar) roughly 60–90 minutes before first warm-up if appetite allows.

- ~10:00 — Warm-up area: start general warm-up (timing relative to first attempt depends on the meet schedule)
  - Note: exact warm-up start is scheduled to hit platform warm-up 10–12 minutes before the attempt. Allow coach to monitor warm-up room barbell availability and adjust.
  - General warm-up (5–8 minutes):
    - Light joint mobility, band pull-aparts, shoulder and hip openers, cat-cow, bodyweight squats, glute bridges. Keep it dynamic and short.
    - 2–3 breathing/bracing cycles to maintain calm.

- Warm-up ramp (in warm-up area): keep sets efficient and focused on technique and feel. Rest long enough between heavy warm-ups so the nervous system is fresh for each ramp. Example ramp for a bench opener at, say, 90kg opener — adapt numbers to her opener.
  - Note: do not perform many heavy warm-up sets with long grinding reps. Focus on singles and doubles that feel crisp.
  - Example bench warm-up progression (adjust for numbers):
    - Bar x 10 (groove/commands)
    - 40% × 5 (tech feel)
    - 60% × 3 (setup practice)
    - 75% × 2 (short pause if needed)
    - 85% × 1 (quick, confident)
    - 92–95% × 1 (opener feel — only if still early in warm-up window; otherwise save opener feel for platform)
  - For squat/deadlift follow similar concise ramp planning. For squats include a few paused or depth-check reps earlier in the ramp; for deadlifts rehearse hook/grip and breathing pattern.

- 10–15 minutes before platform attempt — final platform warm-up and mental cueing
  - Take 1–2 lighter sets or singles at ~70–80% in warm-up area if needed to stay warm, then walk to the platform area.
  - Coach performs final touch-ups: quick cue reminder, breathe, bracing, and “picture” of successful lift.
  - Final short restroom trip and chalk if used.

- On-platform timing
  - Arrive on time for the flight. Platform warm-up may be limited — rely on gym warm-up as main preparation.
  - Use pre-lift routine: two deep breaths, bracing, push foot into floor, aggressive press/drive at the lift.
  - After lift: controlled breathing and positive reinforcement regardless of result; reset for next attempt as needed.

Specific warm-up structure by lift (concise)
- Squat:
  - Mobility & activation: banded hip distractions, ankle circles, bodyweight squat × 8–10
  - Ramp: bar × 5–8, 40% × 3, 60% × 2, 75% × 1–2, 85% × 1, 90% × 1 (optional) — then to platform.
  - Perform 1 rep at opener weight if schedule allows and it feels fast; otherwise trust the ramp.

- Bench:
  - Mobility & activation: band pull-aparts, scap squeezes, light shoulder warm-up.
  - Ramp: bar × 8–10, 40% × 5, 60% × 3, 75% × 2 (paused), 85% × 1, opener single on platform or in warm-up (as schedule allows).

- Deadlift:
  - Mobility & activation: hamstring swings, glute bridges.
  - Ramp: bar × 5–8 (if using trap bar or empty bar reps for speed), 40% × 3, 60% × 2, 75% × 1–2, 85% × 1, opener single on platform (if timing allows).
  - Keep pulls crisp and avoid heavy back stress before platform.

Nutrition and hydration on meet morning
- 2–3 hours pre-lift: main breakfast (small) as above.
- 60–90 minutes pre-lift: small carb snack or sports drink (20–40 g carbs) to top up energy and calm nerves.
- Sip water and electrolyte beverage until 30 minutes before lifting. Avoid large volumes 10–15 minutes before platform to prevent bathroom breaks.
- If athlete uses caffeine, take typical dose 45–60 minutes before platform warm-up begins.

Opener timing strategy (how to pick openers and when to attempt)
- Opener: pick a weight the athlete can hit with good speed for 3 reps in training, typically ~88–92% of 1RM (or whatever the athlete normally uses). The opener’s job is to secure a good start and build confidence.
- Attempt order: use the opening attempt to build momentum — a successful opener calms nerves and prepares for a stronger second attempt.
- Allow 18–25 minutes between warm-up finish and on-platform attempt for recovery and mental reset — exact time depends on meet flow.
- Coach maintains warm-up schedule so warm-up bar moves with the platform flight. Be conservative with time; avoid last-second ramp increases that cause rushed lifts or breathing disruption.

If something goes wrong (missed opener)
- Keep calm and controlled. Use breathing and reset routine. If the miss was technical, coach gives a single focused cue that the lifter has used and trusts.
- If miss is due to timing or blocking — repeat the attempted strategy with small, confidence-building adjustments. Avoid panicked big jumps or drastic changes.

Final checklist for athlete to have in morning bag
- Singlet, socks, shoes, belt, wrist wraps, knee sleeves, lifting chalk, headband/tape if used
- Snacks: banana, energy bar, rice cakes, small bottle electrolytes
- Toiletries/tape/first-aid kit, hand towel, spare shirt, headphones for music, phone with meet schedule and warm-up plan printed or on phone
- Coach contact and warm-up plan sheet with ramp numbers for each attempt

Goals: reduce fatigue, restore CNS and musculature, maintain movement quality, no heavy testing. Keep sessions short and easy, focus on sleep, nutrition, and recovery. Cardio is short and calming.

General deload rules
- Reduce volume by ~50–70% compared to Week 1.
- Keep intensity at 50–70% for most work. If using a single heavier set to keep feel, keep it at RPE 6–7 (roughly 75–80%) and do it only once during the week.

- Accessory work limited to mobility and light activation (2 sets or fewer).

Deload Session A — Squat (Day 8 or 9)
- Warm-up: general mobility 8–10 minutes.
- Ramp: bar × 8, 40% × 5, 55–60% × 3.
- Main: 3 × 3 @ 55–65% focusing on speed, depth, and confidence. Keep pauses, tempo control minimal.

- Main: 3 × 3 @ 55–65% paused or touch-and-go depending on meet requirement; focus on setup and cueing (use her shoulder-set cue lightly).

- Accessory: 2 × 10 face pulls, 2 × 8 light incline DB presses or rows.
- Cardio: 15–20 min easy walk or pool swim later that day (optional).

Deload Session C — Deadlift (Day 12 or 13)
- Warm-up: light hamstring activation and mobility.
- Ramp: empty bar/very light pull × 5–8, 40% × 3, 55–60% × 2.
- Main: 3 × 2 @ 55–65% focusing on smooth setup and hip drive. Keep reps controlled and non-grindy.
- Optional feel single: 1 × 1 @ ~75% RPE 6 (only if desired).
- Accessory: 2 × 8 RDL at light load, 2 × 30s core anti-extension holds.
- Cardio: 20–30 min easy walk on a rest day (do not do same-day intense cardio).

Deload recovery emphasis
- Sleep target: 8+ hours nightly, add naps as needed.
- Nutrition: keep calories at maintenance or slight surplus; prioritize protein and carbs to replenish glycogen and aid recovery.
- Hydration and electrolytes: maintain normal levels; use light sodium supplementation if travel or sweat loss is high.
- Physio/bodywork: schedule a massage, soft-tissue work, or targeted physio session if available.
- Active recovery: daily 10–20 minute easy walk and short mobility; avoid long cardio or high-impact work.

Week 3 — Meet week (Days 15–21) — taper and sharpness
- Very similar to the previously outlined Week 3 but with adjustments because a deload was inserted: athlete should be fresher, so keep the first couple of meet-week sessions very light and only rehearse openers once or twice.
- Schedule:
  - Day 15 (3–5 days before meet): Short squat/tech session — 3–4 sets of 2–3 reps at 50–60% focusing on speed and depth. One light opener rehearsal allowed.
  - Day 17 (2–3 days before meet): Short bench session — 3 × 3 at 50–60% and 1 light opener feel rep if desired.
  - Day 18 (2–3 days before meet): Short deadlift session — 2–3 × 2 at 50–60% and 1 light opener feel rep if desired.
  - Rest and very light walks the last 48 hours. No heavy work.
- Cardio in meet week: keep as short, calm walks (10–20 minutes) on rest days and the day before the meet if it helps sleep and nerves. Avoid anything that raises HR for long periods.

Example workload comparison (illustrative)
- Week 1 main lifts: 1 heavy single @ 90–95% + 2 back-off sets × 3 reps.
- Week 2 deload main lifts: 3 × 3 @ 55–65% (no heavy singles), optional 1 × 1 @ 75% if used.
- Week 3 meet week: 3–4 sets of 2–3 reps @ 50–60% early in the week, then rest.

Coaching and cueing during the deload
- Keep bench shoulder-cue minimal and familiar: do a few light activation reps and band pull-aparts to reinforce the position but do not overhaul grip/mechanics.
- Use the deload to address any mental fatigue: guided breathing, short visualization, and confidence reinforcement.

If the athlete reports lingering fatigue after the deload
- Replace any optional feel singles in Week 3 with additional light technique reps only.
- Keep meet attempts conservative; adjust openers downward slightly to prioritize a successful meet.

Here’s a clear, practical 48‑hour nutrition plan to maximize glycogen, hydration, and readiness without experimenting on race day. Adjust absolute calories and sodium to the athlete’s usual intake, bodyweight, and any weight‑making plan she’s already tested. Don’t try new foods, supplements, or dehydration methods in this period.

Goals
- Replenish and top up muscle glycogen (carbohydrates).
- Ensure optimal hydration and electrolyte balance (fluids + sodium).
- Keep digestion easy and consistent to avoid GI issues on meet day.
- Maintain adequate protein for recovery and muscle repair.

General targets (per day; adjust for bodyweight and tolerance)
- Carbohydrate: moderate–high; aim for ~4–7 g/kg/day across the 48‑hour window, skewed heavier in the 24 hours before the meet. Example for a 65 kg athlete: ~260–455 g carbs/day; aim near the middle (300–400 g) depending on appetite and weight needs.
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day (spread over meals). For 65 kg — ~104–130 g/day.
- Fat: keep moderate but not excessive — 20–30% of calories; avoid very fatty meals immediately pre-meet that slow digestion.
- Fluids: sip consistently to maintain pale urine. Aim for ~2–3 L/day as baseline (more if hot/sweaty or higher body mass).
- Sodium: keep normal-to-slightly-elevated intake (esp. if following carb-loading/salty refeed after weigh-in). Rough target ~2–4 g sodium/day (2,000–4,000 mg) across meals; adjust for sweated losses and personal strategies.

48‑hour timeline and food examples

48–24 hours before the meet
- Carbs: Aim for the higher end of day’s carbs but not an extreme 24‑hour carb overload. Eat balanced meals with 60–70% carbs by calories.
  - Meal examples: oatmeal with banana + honey + yogurt; rice or pasta bowl with lean protein (chicken/fish) and cooked veggies; sandwich or bagel with lean protein and jam/honey.
  - Snacks: rice cakes with jam, banana, dried fruit, sports drink, low‑fat granola or energy bar.
- Protein: include 20–30 g per meal (eggs, Greek yogurt, chicken, fish, whey).
- Fluids: sip water consistently; include electrolyte beverage with meals or during/after training. If using sports drinks, target ~20–40 g carbs per serving for energy + electrolytes as needed.
- Sodium: include normal table salt on meals, eat slightly saltier foods if sweating heavily (olives, pickles, salted nuts, broths).
- Meals: 3 moderate meals + 2–3 carb snacks. Keep fiber and fat moderate to avoid GI upset.

Example day (48–24 h out)
- Breakfast: Oatmeal with banana, honey, Greek yogurt. Coffee if usual.
- Snack mid-morning: Rice cakes + jam or a small energy bar.
- Lunch: Chicken or tofu with white rice or pasta, steamed veggies, drizzle of olive oil, small piece of fruit.
- Snack: Smoothie with fruit + whey or Greek yogurt, plus honey.
- Dinner: Salmon/chicken with mashed potatoes or pasta, small salad (light dressing), bread or roll. Add a cup of chicken broth or miso if stomach allows.
- Fluids: 2–3 L water + 1–2 electrolyte drinks across the day.
- Sodium: moderate; add salt to meals, have salted snack if appetite allows.

24 hours → Meet day morning (last 24 hours)
- Carbs: prioritize carbohydrate quantity and easy-to-digest sources. Move toward 5–7 g/kg if appetite and weight allow (especially if weigh-in already done and she can refeed). If she must weigh in and then refeed, follow her tested rapid refeed strategy.
- Meals: similar structure but favor lower-fiber white carbs (white rice, rice noodles, plain pasta, bagels, white bread, potatoes) to reduce GI bulk.
- Timing: Dinner the night before should be a carbohydrate-focused meal (pasta, potatoes, rice) with moderate lean protein and small fat. Avoid very high-fat or high-fiber meals.
- Evening snack (if needed): small bowl of cereal with milk or a bagel with honey to top up glycogen and aid sleep.
- Fluids: continue sipping; avoid drinking excessively right before bed. Include an electrolyte drink in the evening if the athlete tends to urinate frequently or if the meet is hot.
- Sodium: maintain or slightly increase sodium intake especially if athlete will rehydrate after a weigh-in. A cup of broth, salted nuts, or adding salt to meals helps.

Meet‑morning (within the last 3–4 hours before first lift)
- Meal timing: eat a familiar, carbohydrate-rich meal ~2–4 hours before warm-ups (smaller if stomach sensitive).
- Meal ideas (2–4 hours pre-warm-up): bagel or toast with jam or honey and a little peanut butter; oatmeal with banana and honey; white rice with egg whites and a little soy sauce; pancakes with syrup if tolerated.
- 60–90 minutes pre-warm-up: small carb snack or sports drink (20–40 g carbs) — banana, half a bagel, rice cake with jam, or 200–300 ml sports drink.
- Fluids: sip water and electrolytes up to 30 minutes before warm-up; avoid guzzling right before platform to prevent bathroom issues.
- Sodium: small sodium-containing snack or drink OK (e.g., salted pretzels, broth sips, sports drink) 1–2 hours pre-warm-up to support blood volume and nerve function. If the athlete tends to cramp or feel lightheaded, increase sodium slightly per experience.

Specific sodium guidance
- Normal training days: ~2,000 mg/day is a reasonable baseline.
- If athlete will weigh-in dehydrated and rehydrate after weigh-in: increase sodium after weigh-in aggressively to help retain fluids (add 1–2 g extra sodium post-weigh-in via broth, salty foods, or electrolyte solution). Consult her tested rehydration plan.
- If the venue is hot or the athlete sweats heavily: increase fluid and sodium intake proportionally. Use electrolyte mixes containing sodium (250–500 mg per serving) and aim to replace lost salts.

Practical examples for rehydration after weigh‑in (if applicable)
- Immediately post weigh-in: 300–500 ml electrolyte drink with carbs (e.g., sports drink) + small salty snack (half a sandwich or salty crackers) within 15–30 minutes.
- 90–120 minutes post weigh-in: larger carb meal (rice, pasta, bagel) with protein; sip broths or electrolyte beverage over the next couple of hours.
- Continue to monitor urine color (aim pale straw) and subjective fullness.

- New foods, heavy/fatty meals, very high-fiber meals, and experimental supplements that haven’t been tested.
- Excessive water loading without sodium — this can cause frequent urination and dilute electrolytes.
- Alcohol that interferes with sleep and hydration.
- Excessive caffeine if the athlete is sensitive; stick to usual doses.

- Tailor the exact grams to her bodyweight and whether she must make a weight class. If she has a tested weight-cut/re-feed plan, follow that protocol instead of the generic guidance above.

- Duration: 21 days to meet.

  - Squat day: ramp → 1 × 1 @ ~90–95%; back-off 2 × 3 @ ~80%; 2 light posterior chain accessories; core. Short easy cardio 15–20 min on rest day or later that day if desired.

- Recovery: sleep, nutrition at maintenance/slight surplus, light mobility daily.

- Meet-morning (2–4 hours pre-warm-up): small familiar carb-rich meal (bagel + jam, oatmeal + banana, rice + egg whites). 60–90 min pre-warm-up: 20–40 g carbs snack or sports drink. Sip electrolytes and avoid new foods/supplements.

- Breakfast 2–4 hours pre-warm-up (carb-focused, small). Sip water/electrolytes.

Here’s a concise, coach-ready summary of the revised 3‑week meet prep (with deload + 95% opener rehearsals), including workouts, deload placement, cardio, nutrition highlights, and the meet‑morning plan.

Overview
- Duration: 21 days to meet.
- Structure: Week 1 — peaking start (heavy singles, reduced volume). Week 2 — deload with controlled 95% singles (one per lift mid-week). Week 3 — meet week (very light, sharpen openers, taper).
- Frequency: 3 main lifting days per week (Squat, Bench, Deadlift). Short, easy cardio sessions (walking/bike/pool) 2–4x/wk; scheduled on recovery or evening of lifting days.
- Priority: protect freshness for meet day, rehearse openers at 95% (in deload week per athlete request), limit accessories, emphasize sleep, carbs, and sodium.

Week 1 — Peaking start (Days 1–7)
- Goal: maintain intensity, reduce volume ~50% vs accumulation, practice ramps and technique.
- Sessions (example days 1, 3, 5):
  - Squat day: ramp → 1 × 1 @ ~90–95%; back-off 2 × 3 @ ~80%; 2 light posterior chain accessories; core. Short easy cardio 15–20 min on rest day or later that day if desired.
  - Bench day: ramp → 1 × 1 or 1 × 2 @ ~88–95%; back-off 2 × 3–5 @ ~75–80% (paused if meet requires); short upper-back accessories. Keep bench shoulder-cue light and familiar. Short easy cardio on an off day.
  - Deadlift day: ramp → 1 × 1 @ ~90–95%; back-off 2 × 3 @ ~80%; 1–2 light hamstring/accessory sets; core carry. Short easy cardio on rest day.
- Volume: minimal accessory, total session ~45–60 min.
- Recovery: sleep, nutrition at maintenance/slight surplus, light mobility daily.

Week 2 — Deload + 95% opener rehearsals (Days 8–14)
- Goal: reduce fatigue, rehearse openers at 95% on separate days, stop if any lift feels like an RPE 9+ grinder.
- Structure: schedule one 95% single per lift on separate non-consecutive days (e.g., Squat Day, 48 hrs rest, Bench Day, 48 hrs rest, Deadlift Day).
- Session template for each 95% day:
  - Thorough but conservative ramp (bar → 40% → 60% → 75% → 85% → 95% single).
  - Stop after the 95% single if it moved crisply; follow with 1–2 light, non-fatiguing sets (≤65%). No heavy accessories.
  - Monitor bar speed and RPE; abort further heavy work that week if any single feels excessive.
- All other work in week: main sets at 55–65% for 3 × 2–3 (tech focus) or rest days with mobility and physio. Cardio: very easy walks/bike 10–25 min on recovery days.

Week 3 — Meet week (Days 15–21)
- Goal: sharpness and freshness. Minimal volume, rehearse openers lightly, mental prep.
- Schedule (example):
  - Day 15 (3–5 days pre-meet): short squat/tech session 3–4 × 2–3 @ 50–60% + optional easy opener feel rep.
  - Day 17 (2–3 days pre-meet): short bench session 3 × 3 @ 50–60% + optional easy opener feel rep.
  - Day 18 (2–3 days pre-meet): short deadlift session 2–3 × 2 @ 50–60% + optional easy opener feel rep.
  - Last 48–72 hrs: no heavy lifting; very light walks, mobility, visualization, sleep.
- Cardio: 10–20 minute easy walks or pool swim on rest days; optional short pre-meet day walk to relax.

Nutrition highlights (48 hours + meet morning)
- 48→24 hours: increase carbs to top up glycogen (target ~4–7 g/kg/day across 48 h, skew heavier 24 h before). Eat easy-to-digest carbs (white rice, pasta, bagel), moderate protein (1.6–2 g/kg/day), moderate fat.
- Fluids: sip steadily (≈2–3 L/day baseline). Use electrolyte drinks; increase sodium to ~2–4 g/day across the 48 h if not contraindicated.
- If weigh-in before meet: follow tested refeed/hydration plan — immediately post-weigh-in consume carb + electrolyte beverage and salty carbs (broth, crackers), then a larger carb meal 60–90 min after weigh-in.
- Meet-morning (2–4 hours pre-warm-up): small familiar carb-rich meal (bagel + jam, oatmeal + banana, rice + egg whites). 60–90 min pre-warm-up: 20–40 g carbs snack or sports drink. Sip electrolytes and avoid new foods/supplements.

Meet-morning warm-up & timing (coach-ready)
- Wake early for light movement, bathroom, and 2–3 min visualization.
- Breakfast 2–4 hours pre-warm-up (carb-focused, small). Sip water/electrolytes.
- Arrive early at venue; identify warm-up area and schedule.
- Warm-up progression (concise, lift-specific):
  - General activation 5–8 min (dynamic mobility, band work).
  - Ramp in warm-up area with focused singles/doubles: bar → 40% → 60% → 75% → 85% → opener feel (if schedule allows).
  - Arrive at platform ~8–12 minutes before attempt. Rely on gym ramp for main preparation.
- On-platform: use pre-lift routine (breath, brace, cue). Keep warm-up efficient; avoid extra heavy warm-up sets.
- Opener strategy: conservative opener (a weight she can hit for a confident triple in training); opener secures a lift and builds momentum. Keep planned second and third attempts based on how 95% rehearsals felt.

Cardio prescription during the 3 weeks
- Low-intensity only (RPE ~2–4; 10–30 min). Modalities: brisk walk, easy bike, pool swim, light row.
- Schedule: 2–3 easy sessions Week 1, 2–3 in Week 2 (recovery-focused around 95% days), 1–2 light walks Week 3 (including day before meet).

Key coaching cautions
- 95% singles are rehearsal-only — stop if >RPE 9 or slow bar speed. Prioritize meet readiness over chasing numbers.
- Don’t introduce big technical changes now; keep bench shoulder-cue brief and familiar.
- Monitor sleep, appetite, and soreness — reduce or skip optional opener feels in Week 3 if any residual fatigue.
